title: Quantum Lock-In Detection via Successive Adiabatic Evolution
authors: Kangze Li, Siqi Chen, Hao Zhang, Jiazhao Tian, Liantuan Xiao, Gerardo Adesso
abstract: In recent years, quantum lock-in detection has emerged as a promising technique to accurately detect weak signals submerged in background noise. However, the signal-to-noise ratio of existing protocols is severely limited by spectral leakage resulting from control operations implemented in pulse form. Here, we propose a general protocol for realizing quantum lock-in detection by employing successive quantum adiabatic evolution. In our protocol, the signal modulation is achieved by adiabatically controlling the time evolution of the quantum probe, which enables the implementation of triangular modulation functions. The realization of triangular-wave modulation fundamentally solves the problem of spectral leakage and facilitates the extraction of the complete characteristics of the target signals. We present a practical implementation scheme of adiabatic quantum lock-in detection based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, and demonstrate that the proposed protocol possesses strong resilience against experimental imperfections. Our results establish adiabatic quantum lock-in detection as a robust and experimentally accessible approach to detection of weak alternating signals in noisy environments, thus promoting the advance of real-world quantum sensing technologies.
summary: This paper introduces an advanced quantum protocol for lock-in detection by utilizing successive adiabatic evolution to generate ideal triangular modulation functions. This approach fundamentally overcomes spectral leakage issues present in current methods, enabling the robust and accurate measurement of weak alternating signals. The technique is demonstrated using NV centers in diamond and is presented as a general framework applicable to various controllable quantum systems.
main_problem: The core problem is achieving accurate quantum lock-in detection for weak signals buried in noise, overcoming limitations imposed by spectral leakage inherent in existing pulse-based control protocols.
main_result: The authors propose and demonstrate a general protocol using successive adiabatic evolution that implements triangular modulation, fundamentally solving spectral leakage and providing a robust sensing method.
method: The technique relies on adiabatically controlling the time evolution of a quantum probe through carefully designed sequences of Hamiltonian parameters to extract signal components via accumulated relative phases.
model_or_system: The model uses a driven two-level quantum probe described by a Hamiltonian incorporating control and signal terms. Practical implementations are demonstrated using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, but the protocol is generalizable to other controllable two-level systems.
key_observables: The key observables measured are relative accumulated phases ($\alpha$ and $ eta$) derived from successive quantum evolution steps, which are proportional to integrals involving the unknown signal $M(t)$.
important_parameters: Key parameters include the control field strengths ($\Omega_R(t), \Delta(t)$) and the modulation function shape (achieving triangular profiles). The method is robust against experimental imperfections.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption involves treating the signal coupling term ($H_{	ext{sig}}(t)$) as a weak perturbation during the adiabatic evolution process. It also assumes the applicability of the rotating-wave approximation.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes detail mathematical derivations involving propagators $U(T, 0)$ calculated through sequential application of time-evolution operators for different measurement components ($I_{	ext{sig}}$ and $Q_{	ext{sig}}$).
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the limitations of current quantum sensing methods. It then introduces the general protocol based on successive adiabatic evolution to achieve triangular modulation. The methodology is detailed by deriving the necessary propagators for measuring in-phase and quadrature components, followed by a discussion of its practical realization using NV centers.
why_interesting: This work provides a sophisticated theoretical framework for quantum sensing that directly addresses fundamental limitations (spectral leakage) in measurement protocols. The reliance on adiabatic passage connects concepts from quantum control theory to real-world high-sensitivity measurements, which is highly relevant to AMO physics research.
